talk: Inventory turns count how many times a year you sell through your stock. Stock on a shelf is cash you can't spend, and it can go out of fashion. More turns means less cash stuck and fresher shelves.

terms.meaning: Stock you've paid for but not sold yet.
Cost of the stock sold in a year divided by the average stock you hold.
How many days your stock would last at the current pace.

questions.prompt: Over the year the shop sold stock that cost $600,000. On average you hold $150,000 of stock. How many times a year does stock turn?
questions.hint: Stock sold in a year divided by average stock.
whyNot: At 2 turns you'd only sell 2 x $150,000 = $300,000 of stock a year. You sold $600,000.
6 turns would mean selling 6 x $150,000 = $900,000 of stock. You sold $600,000.
9 turns would mean selling 9 x $150,000 = $1.35M of stock. Far more than the $600,000 you sold.

questions.prompt: Stock turns 4 times a year. Roughly how many days does a typical item sit on the shelf? (Use 365 days.)
questions.hint: Days in a year divided by turns.
whyNot: 30 days on the shelf would mean 365 / 30 = about 12 turns a year. You only turn 4 times.
60 days would mean 365 / 60 = about 6 turns. You turn 4 times.
365 days means stock turns once a year. Yours turns 4 times, so each item sits about a quarter of that.

questions.prompt: You cut average stock to $100,000 and still sell $600,000 a year. How much cash does that free up?
questions.hint: Old stock level minus new stock level.
working: Same sales, $50,000 back in the bank.
whyNot: $100,000 is the new stock level, not the cash freed. You freed the drop: $150,000 - $100,000 = $50,000.
$150,000 was the old stock level. You still hold $100,000 of it.
$600,000 is a year of stock sold. Sales didn't change, only how much sits on the shelf.

penalty.prompt: Over a year the shop sold stock that cost {sold}. On average it holds {avg} of stock. How many times a year does stock turn?
penalty.hint: Stock sold in a year divided by average stock.

traps.why: That's days on the shelf. The question asks for turns a year.

call.title: The slow stock
call.prompt: The shop has $100,000 of old stock that barely sells. A clearance company will buy it for $70,000 cash today. Or you could buy $50,000 more stock to fill the shelves, which should add $1,000 of profit a matchday.

options.label: Clear it for $70,000
options.result: Good call. You take $100,000 - $70,000 = $30,000 less than it cost, but $70,000 is back in the bank and the shelves turn faster.

options.label: Keep it and wait
options.result: Stock that isn't selling is cash you can't use. It won't be worth more next season.

options.label: Buy more stock
options.result: $50,000 / $1,000 = 50 matchdays to earn it back. Buying more slow stock makes the problem bigger.

takeaway: Stock on a shelf is cash you can't spend. Turn it faster.
